questions.q: Under which section is a First Information Report (FIR) recorded under BNSS 2023?
questions.src: Section 173 BNSS corresponds to the old Section 154 CrPC -- FIR registration.

questions.q: What was the equivalent provision for FIR registration under the OLD CrPC, 1973?
questions.src: Section 154 CrPC was the FIR provision, now Section 173 under BNSS.

questions.q: Which section provides for Anticipatory Bail under the BNSS?
questions.src: Section 482 BNSS corresponds to Section 438 CrPC -- Anticipatory Bail.

questions.q: Who can grant anticipatory bail?
questions.src: Anticipatory bail can only be granted by the Sessions Court or High Court, never a Magistrate.

questions.q: Under the old CrPC, Section 125 deals with:
o: Maintenance of wives, children, and parents
questions.src: Section 125 CrPC (now Section 144 BNSS) governs maintenance obligations.

questions.q: Under BNSS, arrest without a warrant is governed by which section, corresponding to Section 41 of the old CrPC?
questions.src: Section 35 BNSS corresponds to Section 41 CrPC on arrest without warrant.

questions.q: A person arrested must be produced before a Magistrate within how many hours, excluding travel time?
questions.src: This is a constitutional requirement (Article 22) mirrored in Section 58 BNSS/Section 57 CrPC.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes registration of an FIR for a COGNIZABLE offence?
o: Police may refuse and require a preliminary inquiry first in every case
Registration is MANDATORY -- police cannot refuse (per Lalita Kumari v. State of U.P.)
Only a Magistrate can register an FIR
FIR can only be filed within 24 hours of the offence
questions.src: Lalita Kumari v. State of U.P. (2014) made FIR registration mandatory for cognizable offences, subject to narrow later exceptions.

questions.q: The genuinely NEW "Zero FIR" provision under BNSS allows:
o: FIR to be filed only at the police station with territorial jurisdiction
FIR to be filed at ANY police station regardless of jurisdiction, later transferred to the correct one
FIR to be filed only online
No FIR to be filed for offences committed abroad
questions.src: Zero FIR removes jurisdictional barriers to initial FIR registration, with later transfer to the appropriate police station.

questions.q: For a NON-cognizable offence, the police:
o: Can arrest without a warrant and investigate freely
CANNOT arrest without a warrant, and need the Magistrate's permission before investigating
Have identical powers to cognizable offences
questions.src: Non-cognizable offences require both an arrest warrant AND magisterial permission to investigate, unlike cognizable offences.

questions.q: "Bailable" vs "Non-Bailable" offences, as distinguished from "Cognizable" vs "Non-Cognizable" offences, are:
o: Exactly the same classification under different names
TWO SEPARATE, independent classifications -- a cognizable offence is not automatically non-bailable
questions.src: These are two independent classification systems -- a frequently tested AIBE trap where candidates wrongly assume one from the other.

questions.q: In a BAILABLE offence, bail is:
o: A MATTER OF RIGHT -- the accused must be released on furnishing bail/bond
questions.src: Section 478 BNSS (Section 436 CrPC) makes bail a matter of right in bailable offences.

questions.q: In a NON-BAILABLE offence, bail is:
o: DISCRETIONARY -- granted or refused by the court based on relevant factors
Impossible to obtain under any circumstances
questions.src: Section 480 BNSS (Section 437 CrPC) makes non-bailable offence bail a matter of judicial discretion.

questions.q: "Default Bail" (or "Statutory Bail") arises when:
o: The accused simply requests it verbally
The chargesheet is NOT filed within the statutory 60 or 90-day period
The accused has a clean prior record
questions.src: Section 187 BNSS (Section 167(2) CrPC) creates a statutory right to bail if investigation/chargesheet filing exceeds the prescribed period.

questions.q: Under the genuinely NEW Section 479 BNSS, a first-time offender who has served how much of the maximum sentence is entitled to release on bond?
questions.src: Section 479 BNSS entitles first-time offenders to release after serving one-third of the maximum sentence, with the jail superintendent required to apply proactively.

questions.q: Section 479 BNSS's first-time offender release provision does NOT apply to offences punishable with:
o: Any offence whatsoever, it applies universally
questions.src: This important carve-out excludes the most serious offences from the accelerated release mechanism.

questions.q: A confession or statement recorded by a Magistrate is governed under BNSS by which section, corresponding to Section 164 CrPC?
questions.src: Section 183 BNSS corresponds to Section 164 CrPC on Magistrate-recorded confessions/statements.

questions.q: A "Pardon" under Section 343 BNSS (Section 306 CrPC) may be tendered ONLY by:
o: A Chief Judicial Magistrate or Metropolitan Magistrate specifically
questions.src: If tendered by an unauthorised Magistrate, the entire proceeding is VITIATED -- a frequently repeated AIBE trap question.

questions.q: Which of the following classifications was ELIMINATED as a distinct designation under BNSS, unlike the old CrPC?
questions.src: BNSS removed the specific "Metropolitan Magistrate"/"Metropolitan Area" designation that existed for large cities under the old CrPC.

questions.q: A "Warrant Trial" applies to offences punishable with imprisonment:
questions.src: Warrant trials handle more serious offences (over 2 years), distinct from Summons Trials for lesser offences.

questions.q: A "Summons Trial" applies to offences punishable with imprisonment:
questions.src: Summons trials are for relatively minor offences with punishment not exceeding 2 years.

questions.q: In D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997), the Supreme Court laid down guidelines primarily addressing:
o: Arrest and custody safeguards to prevent custodial torture
questions.src: D.K. Basu established mandatory safeguards including arrest memos, informing a relative/friend, and medical examination.

questions.q: In Joginder Kumar v. State of U.P. (1994), the Supreme Court held that:
o: Arrest must always happen whenever an offence is lawfully alleged
Arrest is NOT mandatory merely because it is lawful -- it must be justified by genuine necessity
questions.src: This case established that arrest requires genuine necessity, not merely legal permissibility -- a principle now reflected in BNSS's arrest-as-exception approach for offences under 7 years.

questions.q: The maxim "Bail is the rule, jail is the exception" is most associated with which case?
o: Lalita Kumari v. State of U.P.
State of Rajasthan v. Balchand alias Baliay (1977)
D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
Joginder Kumar v. State of U.P.
questions.src: This foundational principle on personal liberty and bail comes from State of Rajasthan v. Balchand.

questions.q: Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022) is significant because it:
o: Called for streamlined, more liberal bail practices, directly influencing BNSS Section 479
Was overturned immediately after being decided
questions.src: This Supreme Court ruling directly shaped the BNSS reform introducing accelerated first-time offender release.

questions.q: The BNSS 2023 contains how many total sections, compared to the CrPC's 484?
questions.src: BNSS has 531 sections, more than the CrPC's 484, reflecting both consolidation and new additions.

questions.q: BNSS 2023 came into force on:
questions.src: BNSS, along with BNS and BSA, came into force on 1 July 2024.

questions.q: Under BNSS, for offences punishable with imprisonment of 3 to 7 years, police may now:
o: Conduct a PRELIMINARY ENQUIRY (with DySP-rank permission) within 14 days before formal FIR registration
Only investigate with a High Court order
questions.src: This is a genuinely new BNSS provision for this specific punishment-severity band, frequently tested as a "what's new" question.

questions.q: The Inherent Powers of the High Court (e.g., to quash an FIR) are governed under BNSS by which section, corresponding to Section 482 CrPC?
questions.src: Section 528 BNSS corresponds to the well-known Section 482 CrPC inherent powers provision.

questions.q: A complainant registering an FIR is entitled to:
o: No copy of the FIR under any circumstances
A FREE COPY of the FIR
A copy only after paying a fee
A copy only if the case goes to trial
questions.src: BNSS confirms the complainant's right to receive a free copy of the registered FIR.
